newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Depressed stock prices spur Singapore takeovers.
newsitem.headline: Depressed stock prices spur Singapore takeovers.

text.p: Depressed share prices in Singapore market have spawned a flurry of true and rumoured corporate takeovers and more can be expected should prices take another plunge, brokers and analysts said on Monday.
The takeover theme took off last year, inspired by Indonesian companies buying major stakes in Singapore-listed companies like L&M Group and ABR, said Vincent Yee, an analyst at Alliance Securities.
"The market is evolving into a new phase where it can't just depend on initial public offerings and fund participation to grow," he said.
On Thursday, Singapore shipping conglomerate Sembawang Corp confirmed one rumour that it was in a takeover move.

Sembawang said as part of a restructuring, it was proposing to make a voluntary takeover offer for all of Sembawang Maritime (SML) shares at S$3.70 (US$2.62) each and all outstanding SML convertible unsecured bonds at S$1.23 each.

Analysts said the move last week was opportunistic as SML's share price had sunk to a low of S$2.96 in mid-August from a high of S$5.20 this year. "In the case of Sembawang Corp making a takeover of Sembawang Maritime, it was the right time to do it," Yee said.
"Now people are wondering if Keppel Corp might do something similar with its unit Steamers Maritime," said one dealer with a foreign broking house.
The dealer said Keppel could buy up Steamers, hive off its profitable telecommunications business for a separate listing later on, and make Steamers its transport arm.

Prior to the Sembawang announcement, the market's focus was on Indonesian counters Transmarco, for which Indonesian businessman Putera Sampoerna has made a conditional offer, and Amcol Holdings, which was being rescued by Indonesian conglomerate Sinar Mas, after being put under judicial management.
Brokers said takeover fever had gripped mostly main board stocks so far this year as foreign investors feel they are giving better value.
They said the market could take a breather for the time being as prices of a number of stocks had surged in anticipation of possible takeovers.
But they expect another round when prices correct sharply.
"When prices fall again, syndicates will spread stories on companies that have some bad news like what happened with Metro," said a dealer.

Punters swallowed the takeover tale spun around retailer Metro on Friday as it had incurred losses in its discount store Kmart while its lucrative property operations were seen as attractive to predators, he said.
"But if you know who owns the company, you will realise the shareholder is not likely to sell," said the dealer.
The rumours propelled Metro to S$6.20 from S$4.22 last Friday. The stock slipped back towards S$5.00 on Monday after the company said it did not know why its share price had jumped.
Singapore brokers said the next round of takeover stories was likely to spill over to second board stocks.
"We are already hearing old stories surrounding second board stocks like Guthrie being revived," said the dealer from the foreign broking house.
